newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Mars rover launch delayed.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Mars rover launch delayed.

text.p: The launch of NASA's first Mars rover was called off early on Tuesday after a ground computer monitoring its rocket failed, NASA officials said.
The McDonnel Douglas Corp. Delta 2 rocket carrying the Mars Pathfinder was due to blast off with the probe at 2:03 a.m. EST (0703 GMT) on Tuesday.
But the countdown was halted with one minute, 33 seconds left to go after a computer monitoring the the rocket's propulsion system lost synchronization.

"We have had a recycle in the countdown due to a console in the block house going out of specification," said NASA launch commentator George Diller. "Because we have no significant launch window today that means that we will scrub for today."
The rocket had to blast off precisely on time to place the probe on course for Mars.
NASA managers were to meet later Tuesday to decide whether another launch attempt could be made at 1:58 a.m. EST (0658 GMT) on Wednesday, Diller said.
NASA has daily launch opportunities until Dec. 31. If the probe is not off the ground by then it will be two years before the planets are suitably aligned again.
The umanned rocket was to carry the probe on the first leg of its 310 million mile (500 million km) interplanetary trek to Mars.

Mars Pathfinder will carry a six-wheeled rover the size of an office laser printer, called Sojourner. Under remote control from earth it will explore the landing site, beaming back pictures of the surface and sniffing out the composition of rocks.
